fact_en: Whether hatched from an egg or born alive, young animals usually look like their parents.
fact_bis: Matawo man gikan sa itlog o buhi, ang mga anak kasagaran kaamgid sa ilang mga ginikanan.
evidence: Title ends on a bare particle with its head noun missing.

fact_en:
Do toads hop around like frogs?

A toad has shorter legs, so it usually crawls or walks more than it jumps.
fact_bis:
Moambak ba ang kabkab sama sa baki?

Ang kabkab naay mas mubo nga mga tiil, mao nga kasagaran ni mokamang o molakaw kaysa moambak.
evidence: Bakulaw is a large ape/bogeyman in Bisaya, not a toad; the body correctly uses kabkab and baki, so the title puts a monster over a toad card.

title_tl: Reseta ng Doktor sa Gamot sa TB
title_bis: Reseta sa Doktor sa Gamot sa TB
fact_en: You can't just buy TB medicine on your own — a doctor must prescribe the right kind and amount for the patient.
fact_bis: Dili puwede nga basta mopalit og tambal sa TB; ang doktor kinahanglan moreseta aron husto ang klase ug gidaghanon sa tambal.
evidence: Gamot again reads as root rather than medicine, while the body uses tambal twice in the same prescription fact.

fact_en: Killing worker ants alone won't stop an invasion — the hidden queen keeps laying eggs. That's why experts use bait the ants carry home, reaching the queen too.
fact_bis: Bisan patyon ang mga trabahante nga hulmigas, mobalik gihapon sila kay padayon nga mangitlog ang tinago nga reyna. Mao nga naggamit ang mga eksperto og paon nga dad-on sa hulmigas balik sa ilang salag, aron maabot usab ang reyna.
evidence: Card is about ant bait reaching the queen, but the title's 'Langgam' is Cebuano for BIRD (the body correctly says 'hulmigas'), so the headline reads 'queen of the bird' — and 'Pait' (bitter) is not bait either.

fact_en: When the weather is hot, we sweat more — so our kidneys make less urine, keeping the body from losing too much water.
fact_bis: Sa init nga panahon, mas mosingot ta — mao nga mas gamay ang ihi, aron dili mahutdan og daghang tubig ang lawas.
evidence: The card is about sweating reducing urine, but 'Bahu' is Cebuano for stink/odour (sweat = 'singot', which the body uses as 'mosingot'), so the title names a smell, not perspiration.

fact_en:
Why is taking the wrong medicine risky?

It can hide your real illness, so the sickness quietly gets worse before you even notice it.
fact_bis:
Nganong peligroso ang sayop nga tambal?

Mahimo niining itago ang tinuod nimong sakit, mao nga molala kini nga wala nimo mahibaw-i.
evidence: 'Gamot' is ROOT in Cebuano (medicine = 'tambal', used in the body), so 'Sayop Gamot Tago Sakit' headlines a wrong root rather than the wrong medicine the card warns about.

title_tl: Buong Kurso ng Gamot sa TB
title_bis: Tibuok Kurso sa Gamot sa TB
fact_en:
Why must you finish all your TB medicine?

You must finish the whole course of TB medicine even after feeling better — stopping early can let the TB come back!
fact_bis:
Ngano nga kinahanglan ubuson ang tibuok tambal sa TB?

Kinahanglan ubuson ang tibuok tambal sa TB bisan kung mibati na ug maayo — kung hunongon dayon, mahimong mobalik ang sakit!
evidence: Title says 'whole course of the ROOT for TB'; the body correctly uses 'tambal' for the TB medicine, making the headline a health-card mismatch.

fact_en: In type 1 diabetes, the pancreas makes little or no insulin — so the person needs to get insulin from outside the body.
fact_bis: Sa type 1 diabetes, halos dili makahimo og insulin ang pancreas — mao nga kinahanglan sa tawo ang insulin gikan sa gawas.
evidence: Title ends on a bare particle with its head noun missing.

fact_en: Many medicines have a 'keep out of reach of children' label and a hard-to-open childproof cap—made that way on purpose so small kids can't accidentally swallow medicine they mistake for candy.
fact_bis: Daghang tambal naa'y pasidaan nga 'ilayo sa mga bata' ug naa'y childproof cap nga lisod ablihan—tinuyo kini aron dili maablihan sa gagmay nga mga bata ug dili sila makainom og tambal nga abi nila kendi.
terms: keep out of reach of children
evidence: 'Childproof Cap sa Gamot' reads as a cap on a plant root in Cebuano; the body consistently uses 'tambal' for the medicine the cap protects children from.

fact_en: Some ants collect seeds and food, then store them inside their nest so they have something to eat on other days.
fact_bis: Naa'y mga hulmigas nga nagatigom og mga liso ug pagkaon sulod sa ilang salag aron adunay makaon sa lain nga adlaw.
evidence: 'Langgam Tipon Salag' tells a Cebuano child that BIRDS store seeds in the nest, while the card and body are about ants ('hulmigas').

fact_en:
Did you know blind fish are kept as pets?

Some people keep blind cave tetras in aquariums! Even without eyes, they don't crash into the glass because they feel the water — hardy and fun to watch swim.
fact_bis:
Nahibal-an ba nimo, adunay tawo nga nag-atiman og buta nga isda?

Adunay mga tawo nga nag-atiman og blind cave tetra sa akwaryum! Bisan walay mata, dili sila mabangga sa salamin kay mabati nila ang tubig — lig-on ug nindot tan-awon nga molangoy.
evidence: Cebuano 'bulag' means to separate/part ways (blind = 'buta', which the body uses: 'buta nga isda'), so the headline reads 'separated fish' instead of blind cave fish.

fact_en:
Why do babies have soft spots on their head?

Babies' skull bones haven't fully closed yet — those soft spots let them be born safely and give the brain room to grow. They close up as the baby gets older.
fact_bis:
Nganong humok ang ulo sa masuso?

Wala pa hingpit nasira ang bukog sa bungo sa masuso — nakatabang kini aron luwas silang matawo ug adunay luna nga motubo ang utok. Mosira kini samtang motigulang sila.
evidence: 'Lumot' is moss/algae in Cebuano (102 corpus bodies use it that way); the soft spot is 'humok' in this card's own body, so the title reads 'baby's fontanelle moss'.
